title: Lemon balm
subtitle: The lemon-scented kitchen herb for nerves, sleep, and cold-sore skin
excerpt: Lemon balm is the lemon-scented herb of the kitchen garden, traditionally taken for anxious nerves, restless sleep, and cold sore outbreaks. Gentle enough for everyday cups, it sits between the calming herbs and the mild antivirals in the western herbal tradition. Dried leaves keep a year in a cupboard.
sourceNotes: Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931), lemon balm entry, Botanical.com transcription. Culpeper's Complete Herbal (1653), balm entry, public domain. EMA HMPC monograph on Melissa officinalis (2013), open access, dosing and thyroid reference. British Herbal Pharmacopoeia (1983), melissa section.

glossaryTerms.definition: A property traditionally associated with inhibiting viral activity. In lemon balm this is specifically linked to rosmarinic acid and its effect on the herpes simplex virus that causes cold sores.

content.text: Lemon balm in the home kitchen is the lemon-scented leaf that makes a light, refreshing tea and has a long record as the kitchen-garden remedy for a wound-up mind, a wakeful night, and the occasional cold-sore outbreak. The fresh leaf smells strongly of lemon; the dried leaf is gentler but still recognisable. Western herbal practice draws on it as a
nerve-calming herb
: a calming herb that eases anxiety and restlessness without sedating heavily. A jar of dried lemon balm keeps a year in the kitchen cupboard.
Precautions
Not medical advice. Consult a qualified herbalist or doctor for ongoing or serious symptoms.

Thyroid medication: high doses of lemon balm have been studied for their effect on thyroid activity. Readers on thyroid hormone replacement (levothyroxine or equivalent) should consult their prescriber before taking concentrated preparations of lemon balm regularly, as the herb may affect thyroid function at high doses. One or two cups of tea per day at standard infusion strength is unlikely to be a problem, but tinctures and high-dose extracts sit in the cautious column.
Botanical

Melissa officinalis, family Lamiaceae. Lemon balm is a bushy perennial herb with crinkled, bright-green leaves and a strong lemon scent when rubbed. It produces small white flowers in midsummer. Parts used are the leaf and the aerial parts, harvested just before or at the point of flowering when the volatile oil content is highest. The plant naturalises easily in the UK, growing in sun or partial shade and self-seeding freely once established. It is one of the easiest kitchen herbs to grow.
active compounds and actions

The main active compounds are rosmarinic acid, citral, and a range of flavonoids. The calming action is linked to the flavonoids and rosmarinic acid working on GABA pathways in the nervous system. At tea doses the effect is mild and calming. Combined with valerian or passionflower, lemon balm is long used for sleep where the main obstacle is an overactive mind.

The antiviral action of lemon balm is linked to rosmarinic acid and its effect on herpes simplex virus. Limited trial evidence supports lemon balm cream applied to cold sores at the first tingle: it may reduce duration and severity. Internal lemon balm tea does not have the same concentrated topical effect at the site of infection.
Traditional uses

Western herbal practice has used lemon balm as a calming herb since at least the medieval period. The main uses are anxiety, nervous tension, restless sleep, nervous headache, and the digestive upset that comes with stress. The herb is considered gentle enough for everyday cups and for older children under guidance.

The folk European kitchen tradition uses lemon balm as a bee plant and a lemon flavouring for cordials. It is also a reliable calming tea. The cold-sore link is specific to western herbal tradition and tied to late twentieth century antiviral research.
Preparations

A hot infusion is the standard preparation: one to two teaspoons of dried leaf per cup, covered with just-off-boil water, steeped covered for ten minutes. Cover the cup: the lemon-scented volatile fraction is part of the preparation and is lost from an uncovered cup. Fresh leaf makes a more fragrant cup, though the concentration of rosmarinic acid is similar. A cooled strong infusion applied to the lip at the first tingle of a cold sore is the topical use. concentrated creams standardised to rosmarinic acid are the preparation with the most clinical evidence behind them.

A lemon balm alcohol extract provides a stronger, longer-shelf-life preparation than dried leaf. It combines well with passionflower or valerian in sleep and anxiety formulas. As dried herb it combines well with chamomile for a gentler everyday digestive and calming tea.
Cautions and cautions

Thyroid activity at high doses: lemon balm has been studied for its effect on hyperthyroid conditions. And high doses may affect thyroid hormone levels. Readers on levothyroxine or other thyroid hormone replacement should consult their prescriber before regular use of concentrated preparations. Standard cups of tea at one or two per day are unlikely to be a concern. But if you are on thyroid medication and want to use lemon balm regular, a quick conversation with your prescriber is sensible.

No significant drug effect have been documented at culinary-tea doses. The herb has a long history of use without significant adverse event reports at customary doses. Making it one of the more accessible nerve-calming herbs for everyday use.
